unmerge → edit → re-merge, which is what this does for you. Notion does not
support merging at all.

## Data model

Spans live on the anchor as `colSpan`/`rowSpan`, absent meaning one, so a diagram
saved before merging existed is already correct. The cells a merge swallows stay
in the array, keeping the grid rectangular so every index into it still means
what it did. Which cells are covered is **derived** from the anchors, not
flagged — a flag and the span it mirrors are two things that can disagree.

This also answers the open question in #520. A span composes with a later field
pointing at a child node, so a cell that both spans and contains is just an
anchor carrying both. The two features do not need settling together.

## The worksheet

`libraries/packs/worksheets/stride-worksheets`, one template: **STRIDE per
Interaction**. Two elements and the flow between them, a row per STRIDE
category, a Mitigations/Weaknesses pair per element.

**Greyed cells are semantic, not styling** — the categories that do not apply to
that element type, from Vikram's heuristic in #520 (external entity: T, I, D, E;
data store: S, E; data flow: S, R, E; process: none). Grey therefore means "not
applicable" throughout the worksheet, which is why the header rows are yellow: a
grey header would read as a struck-out row.

**`pack_type: template`, not `full`.** It carries no components, threats or
countermeasures. A worksheet is a method rather than a technology domain, so it
has nothing to contribute to the suggestion engine and nothing to join against a
taxonomy — it is complete as it stands, not an unfinished pack.

## Template packs are offered without being connected

`DFDTemplatesLibraryViewSet.get_queryset` gated every template on its source
pack being connected to the threat model, so the `component_ref`s in it resolve;
an AWS template inserted without the AWS pack yields components pointing at
nothing. A template pack ships no components, so a connection has nothing to
supply, and gating it would make a facilitator connect a STRIDE worksheet to
their model as though it described their stack. Those packs are now exempt.

I traced the path from pack YAML to canvas and called it a passthrough before
finding this, which was wrong — the gate sits in a queryset upstream of every
hop I looked at. It only turned up by inserting the template against a running
stack.

## Bugs fixed here

**Merged cells were not clickable through the middle.** Divider drag strips span
the whole table, so the strip for the boundary between two merged rows lay across
the centre of the merged cell — exactly where a pointer lands — and started a row
resize instead. Dividers are now emitted in runs that skip any boundary a merge
crosses. Found by a test timing out on `cursor-row-resize … intercepts pointer
events`; it would have shipped otherwise.

**Arrow keys walked into merged blocks.** Stepping right from a two-wide merge
landed on a covered cell, which renders nothing, so the selection appeared to
vanish. The covered map carries each cell's anchor, and `moveFocus` steps out of
the whole block rather than one cell at a time.

stayed open until a click landed outside the table; an unselected one was fine,
since only a selected table takes the pointer at all. React's `stopPropagation`
stops the native event at the root container, and Radix dismisses layers from a
`pointerdown` listener on `document` above it. Nothing needed the stop: `nodrag`
is what keeps a press from dragging the node, and no ancestor of a cell handles
`pointerdown` (@xyflow/react 12.10.0 — its only React-level one is on `Handle`, a
descendant, and the pane's is capture-phase).

- `npx playwright test` — 36 passed, including a regression test for the menu
  that fails on the previous commit (`toBeHidden` → received visible).
- `manage.py test apps.diagrams.tests.test_template_pack_visibility` — 2 passed,
  covering both halves: the template pack is offered unconnected, and every other
  pack is still gated.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint` clean on every file touched.
- Inserted the worksheet from the template browser against a running stack, with
  the pack imported and deliberately not connected to any threat model — the
  state a real user is in.

## Look hardest at

- `expandRangeOverMerges`. Merging a range that cuts an existing merge would
  leave two anchors claiming one cell, which nothing downstream can render. It
  grows the range to swallow whole merges, iterated to a fixed point because
  widening to absorb one can bring the edge against another.
- The queryset relaxation. Widening it further would break technology templates
  quietly, which is why the second test matters more than the first.
- The divider runs, which are the least obvious part of the diff and exist only
  because of the click-stealing bug above.

- Merging is not offered across a selection that is already partly merged in a
  way the expansion cannot resolve; it simply widens instead. No case found where
  that is wrong, but it is the area I would fuzz first.
- The guest editor gets no templates, deliberately, so the worksheet is not
  reachable there.
- Reassigning a worksheet column group to a different element type means
  re-greying its column pair by hand. The greys are keyed to the three types the
  template ships with.

into a filled column arrives unfilled. That is visible, and the alternative
was resolving cell over column over row on every render and giving "clear
this cell" two meanings.

shrinks the rectangle from a fixed anchor. Before this the arrows reached
React Flow and nudged the whole table instead, which is still what they do
when no cell is selected — one click selects the node, a second selects a
cell, and only then do the arrows belong to the table.

Shift works here although shift-click does not. React Flow's
`selectionKeyCode` swallows a pointerdown while Shift is held but leaves
keydowns alone, so the keyboard route to a multi-cell selection was open
even though the pointer one was not.

out of a dragged range has to leave from the end the pointer finished on,
and reversing a shift-arrow has to shrink the selection back through itself

the next click overwrites both. "No fill" is a distinct third state and is
marked: an unfilled cell says so.

exactly the place it matters most — telling an unfilled cell apart from a
picker with nothing chosen. One ring covers all nine.

one is announced. Set as props on the menu item rather than by switching to

Interaction**. Two elements and the flow between them, a row per STRIDE
category, a Mitigations/Weaknesses pair per element.

**Greyed cells are semantic, not styling** — the categories that do not apply to
that element type, from Vikram's heuristic in #520 (external entity: T, I, D, E;
data store: S, E; data flow: S, R, E; process: none). Grey therefore means "not
applicable" throughout the worksheet, which is why the header rows are yellow: a
grey header would read as a struck-out row.

**`pack_type: template`, not `full`.** It carries no components, threats or
countermeasures. A worksheet is a method rather than a technology domain, so it
has nothing to contribute to the suggestion engine and nothing to join against a
taxonomy — it is complete as it stands, not an unfinished pack.

## Template packs are offered without being connected

`DFDTemplatesLibraryViewSet.get_queryset` gated every template on its source
pack being connected to the threat model, so the `component_ref`s in it resolve;
an AWS template inserted without the AWS pack yields components pointing at
nothing. A template pack ships no components, so a connection has nothing to
supply, and gating it would make a facilitator connect a STRIDE worksheet to
their model as though it described their stack. Those packs are now exempt.

I traced the path from pack YAML to canvas and called it a passthrough before
finding this, which was wrong — the gate sits in a queryset upstream of every
hop I looked at. It only turned up by inserting the template against a running
stack.

## Bugs fixed here

**Merged cells were not clickable through the middle.** Divider drag strips span
the whole table, so the strip for the boundary between two merged rows lay across
the centre of the merged cell — exactly where a pointer lands — and started a row
resize instead. Dividers are now emitted in runs that skip any boundary a merge
crosses. Found by a test timing out on `cursor-row-resize … intercepts pointer
events`; it would have shipped otherwise.

**Arrow keys walked into merged blocks.** Stepping right from a two-wide merge
landed on a covered cell, which renders nothing, so the selection appeared to
vanish. The covered map carries each cell's anchor, and `moveFocus` steps out of
the whole block rather than one cell at a time.

**The context menu would not close over a selected table** — this one shipped in
#553. A selected table swallowed the pointerdown on its cells, so an open menu
stayed open until a click landed outside the table; an unselected one was fine,
since only a selected table takes the pointer at all. React's `stopPropagation`
stops the native event at the root container, and Radix dismisses layers from a
`pointerdown` listener on `document` above it. Nothing needed the stop: `nodrag`
is what keeps a press from dragging the node, and no ancestor of a cell handles
`pointerdown` (@xyflow/react 12.10.0 — its only React-level one is on `Handle`, a
descendant, and the pane's is capture-phase).

## Verification

- `npx playwright test` — 36 passed, including a regression test for the menu
  that fails on the previous commit (`toBeHidden` → received visible).
- `manage.py test apps.diagrams.tests.test_template_pack_visibility` — 2 passed,
  covering both halves: the template pack is offered unconnected, and every other
  pack is still gated.
- `npx tsc --noEmit` and `npx eslint` clean on every file touched.
- Inserted the worksheet from the template browser against a running stack, with
  the pack imported and deliberately not connected to any threat model — the
  state a real user is in.

## Look hardest at

- `expandRangeOverMerges`. Merging a range that cuts an existing merge would
  leave two anchors claiming one cell, which nothing downstream can render. It
  grows the range to swallow whole merges, iterated to a fixed point because
  widening to absorb one can bring the edge against another.
- The queryset relaxation. Widening it further would break technology templates
  quietly, which is why the second test matters more than the first.
- The divider runs, which are the least obvious part of the diff and exist only
  because of the click-stealing bug above.

## Left out

- Merging is not offered across a selection that is already partly merged in a
  way the expansion cannot resolve; it simply widens instead. No case found where
  that is wrong, but it is the area I would fuzz first.
- The guest editor gets no templates, deliberately, so the worksheet is not
  reachable there.
- Reassigning a worksheet column group to a different element type means
  re-greying its column pair by hand. The greys are keyed to the three types the
  template ships with.

issue.title: feat(cyclonedx): complete satisfies/externalReferences import + POA&M tracking
issue.body:
## Why this matters (plain language)

Precogly can already import CycloneDX Threat-Model BOMs (TM-BOMs), but the importer today drops several fields that FedRAMP / SSPP-style workflows depend on: which NIST control a countermeasure claims to satisfy, the evidence URL for each control, and Plan-of-Action-and-Milestones (POA&M) tracking (`poam:id`, scheduled completion date, whether a control is overdue). Users generating a TM-BOM from a compliance tool and importing it into Precogly currently lose that context and have to re-enter it by hand.

This PR closes those gaps so a TM-BOM round-trips through Precogly with its compliance and POA&M metadata intact.

## Value

- Enables using Precogly as the visualization/threat-analysis layer for teams whose source of truth is a CycloneDX TM-BOM (GSA SSPP flow, FedRAMP submissions, etc.) without losing control-mapping fidelity.
- Adds first-class POA&M fields on `InstanceCountermeasure`, so overdue controls surface in the API without a custom join.

## What this changes

- **POA&M fields on `InstanceCountermeasure`**: `poam_id`, `scheduled_completion`, and a `source` enum (`manual` / `vault_import` / `pentest`), plus a `days_overdue` property that ignores `IMPLEMENTED` / `VERIFIED` controls. The CycloneDX importer parses `poam:id` and `poam:scheduled-completion` control properties.
- **`satisfies[]` import**: imports `definitions[].requirements`, creates `InstanceCountermeasureStandard` rows for each control's `satisfies[]`, resolving `StandardRequirement` FK when the framework is installed. When the framework isn't installed, we keep section_code / framework_name / description snapshots so the mapping still displays and round-trips on export. Dangling references warn and skip. Multiple unresolved mappings per control are all preserved (previously only the last survived).
- **`externalReferences` import**: a control externalReference typed `evidence` populates `InstanceCountermeasure.evidence_url`.
- **`crosses_trust_zone`**: `DataFlow` imported from `blueprint.flows` sets `crosses_trust_zone` when source and destination sit in different trust zones.
- Refactors requirement-snapshot construction into a single helper.

Closes tracking issues in GSA-TTS/TTSE-petrified-forest-sspp#31.

## Independence

- Migration `threats/0015_poam_fields` is additive and independent (numbered above current `main`'s `threats/0014`).
- Files touched are disjoint from PRs #560 (packs/systems/frontend icon), #561 (compliance app), and #551 (docker-compose overlay). Safe to merge in any order relative to those.

## Testing

- `backend/apps/threats/tests/test_poam_fields.py` — POA&M model fields, `days_overdue`, API filters.
- `backend/apps/threat_models/tests/test_cdx_poam_import.py` — CycloneDX `poam:*` property parsing on import.
- `backend/apps/threat_models/tests/test_cdx_import_audit.py` — resolved/unresolved/dangling satisfies, evidence-url mapping, zone-crossing flags, satisfies round-trip.
- Full backend suite: `345 passed` (no regressions).
- `manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run`: no missing migrations.
- `ruff check`: clean.

## Draft note

Marked draft — awaiting a first pass of upstream review on the `satisfies[]` snapshot-vs-resolved contract (do we prefer snapshot-only when the framework isn't installed, or block the import?). Happy to switch behavior if reviewers want stricter semantics.

issue.title: feat(packs): pack-level icon via safe SVG-file loading
issue.body: ## Why this matters (plain language) Precogly's DFD nodes render a technology icon next to the node label — for example, an S3 bucket shows an S3 logo. Today only individual components in a pack can declare an icon; the pack itself can't. That means threat libraries and template packs (which have a strong brand identity — "AWS", "Azure", "OWASP") show a generic square in the UI, and components without their own icon have no visual context for which pack they came from. This PR gives packs a first-class icon field and lets components without their own icon fall back to their pack's icon. Everything renders through the existing safe base64-`` pipeline introduced by the #516 XSS fix — no new rendering path and no new npm dependency. ## Value - Restores brand context in the DFD editor (AWS pack components look like AWS things even if a specific service has no bespoke icon yet). - Same XSS-safety guarantee as the existing per-component icon mechanism — pack-supplied SVGs are never injected as raw HTML. - No new frontend dependency. No new backend dependency. Migration is a single additive `TextField`. ## Context on the earlier attempt An earlier branch (`feature/icon-library-mvp`) tried to add pack icons by introducing `@thesvg/react`, a JSON icon config (slug / variant / className / style), and raw-SVG-component rendering. It was written before #516 landed. Merging it as-is would (a) re-introduce a raw-markup icon rendering path that #516 deliberately removed, and (b) run two incompatible icon pipelines side-by-side. This PR keeps the value (pack + component-level fallback) by extending the *existing, already-reviewed* mechanism one level up, from component to pack. Not carried over: per-component icon JSONField overrides, vendor-brand-logo resolution via `@thesvg/react`, and the dual vendor+service icon render. Re-adding equivalents needs a fresh design that keeps the base64-`` constraint. Happy to scope that as a follow-up. ## What this changes **Backend** - `LibraryPack.icon_svg` (`TextField`, same shape as `ComponentLibrary.icon_svg`), migration `packs/0003_librarypack_icon_svg`. - Pack importer reads an optional `pack.yaml` `icon: ` (relative to the pack dir), mirroring the existing per-component `icon: ` convention in `components.yaml`. Missing files warn; nothing throws. - `LibraryPackListSerializer` / `LibraryPackDetailSerializer` expose `icon_svg` (viewset is `ReadOnlyModelViewSet`, so no write path is added). - `ComponentLibrarySerializer` gains `source_pack_icon_svg` so a component without its own icon can fall back to its pack's icon. **Frontend** - `ComponentLibraryItem.sourcePackIconSvg`; `transformToTechnology` and `ComponentPanel` fall back to it. - Everything still flows through the existing `SvgIcon` component (base64 data-URI ``, never `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`). **Docs** - `creating-library-packs.md` documents the `pack.yaml` `icon:` key and explains why it's safe. ## Independence - Migration `packs/0003_librarypack_icon_svg` is additive and independent. - Files touched are disjoint from PRs #559 (threats/cyclonedx), #561 (compliance app), and #551 (docker-compose overlay). Safe to merge in any order relative to those. ## Testing - Backend: `ruff check` clean; new `apps/packs/test_pack_icon_svg.py` (4 tests) + full `apps/packs`, `apps/systems`, and template-pack-visibility suite (51 total) pass; `makemigrations --check --dry-run` reports no changes. - Frontend: `tsc --noEmit` and `eslint` clean on touched files.

issue.title: feat(compliance): JSON/HTML compliance-matrix endpoint per threat model
issue.body:
## Why this matters (plain language)

Compliance reviewers (SSPP authors, FedRAMP assessors, security engineers) need to see, for a given threat model, which NIST-800-53 controls are covered by which countermeasures — and which controls have nothing pointing at them. Today Precogly stores all the underlying data (`StandardRequirement`, `InstanceCountermeasureStandard`, `CountermeasureThreatLink`, plus `ctrl_id` in threat metadata), but there's no single endpoint that puts it together into a per-threat-model matrix.

This PR adds a read-only endpoint that returns exactly that: one row per control, with the countermeasures satisfying it, the threats mapped to it, and provenance for each mapping. There's a JSON API for programmatic use and an HTML variant for browser preview.

## Value

- Turns Precogly into a viable "single pane of glass" for SSPP-style compliance-matrix reviews without leaving the tool.
- No schema change — pure read-side. Safe to add on top of any tenant's existing data.
- Multi-tenancy is honored via `ThreatModel.visible_to`, so a user hitting a threat model outside their scope gets 404, not a data leak.

## What this changes

- New endpoints:
  - `GET /api/threat-models/<tm_id>/compliance-matrix/?framework=<name>` — JSON, default framework `NIST 800-53 Rev 5`.
  - `GET /api/threat-models/<tm_id>/compliance-matrix.html` — HTML render of the same payload.
- Row schema: one row per `StandardRequirement`, grouped by control family (AC, AU, CM, ...), each row projects countermeasures + threats with sufficiency and provenance.
- Threat-side `ctrl_id` fallback: reads `ComponentInstanceThreat.format_metadata['cyclonedx']['ctrl_id']` (and the `DataFlowInstanceThreat` equivalent), so threats generated by the CycloneDX SSPP flow that carry a control id directly still surface — interim until a first-class `ThreatStandard` model lands.
- `include_empty` query flag to show controls with no mapping (drives the "gap" view in SSPP review).
- Golden JSON snapshot fixture committed as `tests/fixtures/matrix_snapshot.json` to pin the payload contract.

## Split note

The fork branch this came from (`feat/compliance-matrix-view`, identical to `feat/cloudgov-keycloak-sso`) also carried cloud.gov / Keycloak SSO and podman-compose changes. Those are unrelated and are being landed separately (podman is PR #551). This PR isolates just the compliance-matrix commits onto current `main`. The `uv.lock` entries the cherry-pick pulled in for the SSO deps were dropped in a follow-up commit — this PR adds no new Python dependencies.

## Independence

- No schema change; no migration.
- Files touched are disjoint from PRs #559 (threats/cyclonedx), #560 (packs/systems/frontend icon), and #551 (docker-compose overlay). Safe to merge in any order relative to those.

## Testing

- `ruff check` clean on touched files.
- `apps/compliance` suite (14 tests) passes; full backend suite (333 tests) passes with no regressions.
- `makemigrations --check --dry-run`: no changes.

521.message:
chore(ui): add a context menu primitive

Wraps @radix-ui/react-context-menu the way dropdown-menu.tsx wraps its own
primitive, rather than pulling the file in through the shadcn CLI, so the
styling stays in step with the components already here.

Needed by the canvas table's row and column controls, where right-click is
the discoverable route to insert and delete: Notion, FigJam, Google Docs
and Word all put those operations there.

feat(dfd-editor): add a table node type to the canvas

An annotation node, like the sticky note: it carries no DFD semantics and
is excluded from threat analysis. Cells hold text, edited in place with
Tab and Enter moving between them. Column and row dividers resize, grips
along the top and left edges select a row or column, and right-clicking
any cell or grip offers insert and delete. Corner handles scale the whole
table, with shift constraining to a uniform factor and taking the cell
text size with it, as Miro does.

A cell is an object rather than a bare string so that it can later hold a
diagram node -- draw.io-style container tables -- without migrating every
saved diagram.

The table derives its size from its own column widths and row heights, so
it is created without style dimensions and React Flow measures it. That is
also why NodeResizer is not used for the corner handles: it wants to own
style.width, and two owners of one dimension start disagreeing.

Pointer deltas in both the divider and corner drags are divided by the
canvas zoom, because sizes are stored in diagram coordinates and a drag at
50% zoom must move twice as far in the data as on screen. Both drags keep
their sizes in local state and commit once on pointerup, so a drag is one
undo entry rather than one per pixel.

There is deliberately no upper bound on a table's size, and the cost is
unpaid for: every cell is a DOM node with no virtualization, so a 20x200
table is 4000 elements the canvas walks on every pan and zoom. If large
tables turn out to be common the fix is to virtualize, not to add a limit.

Two things here are not about tables:

The three node type registries now assert exhaustiveness with `satisfies
Record<DiagramNodeType, unknown>`. React Flow substitutes its default node
for an unregistered type, which renders as a small box containing the
label -- it reads as a broken component rather than a missing entry, and
cost an afternoon before the guard existed.

`nodeSupportsComponentThreats` replaces a condition that was duplicated
across both editors and about to grow a third term, and records why each
type is excluded: trust zones because their threats attach to the
boundary, annotations because they have no DFD semantics.

feat(dfd-editor): choose a table's size when inserting it

Clicking Table in the component panel opens a grid picker: hover to
highlight a rectangle from the top left, click to insert that size. An
input mode keeps the grid on screen as a live preview of the typed numbers
and reaches sizes the 8x8 grid cannot express, clamping its highlight to
the grid's bounds so 17 rows shows as all 8 filled.

Dragging the palette entry still drops a default 3x3. A drag has nowhere
to carry the size choice, so click and drag deliberately differ.

Free-text counts are safe here in a way they are not in the edit panel:
the table does not exist yet, so a half-typed "1" on the way to "12" has
no cells to truncate. The panel uses steppers for that reason.

feat(dfd-editor): wrap text in table cells

Cell text was clipped with an ellipsis because a row's height was exactly
its stored height, so wrapped text would have overflowed its row. Follow
Miro instead: a stored height becomes a floor, and `minmax(h, auto)` lets
the row grow when its content needs more. Two consequences come with that
rule, both of which Miro shares -- dragging a row divider above the
content's own height has no visible effect, and scaling the table down
cannot shrink a row below what its text needs.

A row's real height is therefore no longer knowable from the data, so
every per-row and per-column control moves into the grid rather than being
positioned from a running sum of stored heights. Grips and dividers now
place themselves in a track and push their visible part outside it with
`bottom: 100%` / `right: 100%`, so they track the real geometry with no
measurement pass and nothing to drift. `columnOffsets`, `rowOffsets`,
`totalWidth` and `totalHeight` are gone; the container shrink-wraps the
grid, which lets the corner handles and append buttons anchor to its edges
instead of computing pixels.

The alternative was a ResizeObserver reporting actual row heights back to
the absolutely positioned overlays. Rejected: it keeps the offset
arithmetic and adds a frame where the overlays are stale, where placing
them in the grid deletes the arithmetic and makes the misalignment
impossible rather than merely corrected.

Cells are edited in a textarea rather than an input, so editing wraps the
way the rendered cell does instead of scrolling one long line, and the
cell no longer changes shape on every double-click. Shift-enter inserts a
deliberate line break; plain enter still moves down the column. The
textarea is sized to its content on every keystroke, as InlineEditableLabel
already does for node labels -- without it the box stays one line tall
while being typed into and the row only grows once editing ends.

Cells are now placed explicitly in the grid. The dividers are grid items
with definite positions and a column divider spans `1 / -1` of its column,
so between them they claim every defined cell; auto-placed cells were
pushed into implicit rows below the table and collapsed to nothing.

docs(dfd-editor): correct the table comment that wrapping invalidated

TableNodeData claimed outer height is the sum of row heights. That stopped
being true when rows became `minmax(h, auto)`: a row grows past its stored
height to fit wrapped text, so the sum is a lower bound. The comment also
predated the corner handles and named only the dividers as the way to
resize.

The rest is prose. No behaviour changes.

refactor(dfd-editor): split the table node's drag gestures and chrome out

TableNode was 770 lines against 249 for the next largest file in nodes/.
Some of that is intrinsic -- every other node there renders a shape with a
label, while this one does grid layout, in-cell editing, keyboard
navigation, two pointer gestures, a row/column selection model and a
context menu. Two blocks were not.

`useTableDrag` takes the divider and corner drags, 159 lines of pointer
arithmetic with no JSX. They belong together because they share a shape --
sizes held locally and committed once on pointerup, deltas divided by the
canvas zoom -- which is now stated once in the hook rather than twice in
two handlers. The hook owns the draft state and returns the effective
sizes, so the component lost two useState declarations along with the
handlers.

`table-chrome` takes the geometry constants and the controls drawn around
the table. The grips earn it: the column and row versions were ~90 lines
differing only by axis, and one component means a fix cannot land in one
and miss the other.

The cell and its context menu stay inline. Extracting them means eight
props to move a hundred lines, and that contract reads worse than the
version it replaces.

Also here, because they were entangled in the same lines:

Magic numbers named. `h-[18px]`, `-right-[22px]` and a bare 6 inside a
calc become BUTTON and GAP, beside the GRIP, HANDLE and DIVIDER_HIT that
already existed. The four small action buttons were carrying an identical
ten-class string each; they are now one component.

Two effects rewritten to React's set-during-render pattern -- seeding the
caret on a fresh drop, and dropping the axis selection when the node is
deselected. Both derive local state from a changed prop, which an effect
does a render late. They had been violating the rule all along: extracting
a second component into the file stopped the React Compiler lint bailing
out, and it started reporting them.

issue.title: Component and flow threat lists truncate at 20
issue.body:
`useComponentThreats` (`frontend/src/features/threat-models/api/threats.ts:145`) and `useFlowThreats` (`:170`) keep only `results` from a paginated response. A component with more than 20 threats shows 20 in threat analysis, with no indication the list is short.

`ComponentInstanceThreatViewSet` (`backend/apps/threats/views.py:227`) and `DataFlowInstanceThreatViewSet` set no `pagination_class`, so both take the project default and paginate at 20.

Same bug as #484, on the threat analysis path instead of the Risk Register.

## Not currently reproducible

Seeded components carry at most 4 threats:

```
components with threats: 11
top component threat counts: [4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 4, 3, 3]
components over 20 threats: 0
```

(measured 2026-09-09 against a fresh seed)

It needs a component dense enough to cross 20 — an imported model, or several library packs on one component.

## Expected

Load every page for this list, or surface pagination as #484 does for the register. Either way, the count shown should be the count of threats on the component.

#512 adds `getPage<T>()` in `frontend/src/lib/api.ts`, which returns the whole `Page` and normalizes both response shapes.

512.message:
feat(core): let API clients choose a page size

Stock PageNumberPagination leaves page_size_query_param unset, so PAGE_SIZE is
the only page size any client can get. The Risk Register's board groups a page
into columns; a column count describes the register only when the page holds it.

max_page_size bounds the request, without which ?page_size=999999 asks the server
to serialize an entire table. A caller that asks for no size still gets PAGE_SIZE,
so no existing endpoint changes shape.

The page-size tests fail against stock PageNumberPagination. The rest pass either
way, pinning the DRF behavior the frontend depends on.

fix(threat-models): paginate the Risk Register

useRisks kept only `results` and discarded `count`, so a register of 24 risks
loaded 20 and reported 20. The remaining four were unreachable, and selection and
bulk actions operated on the first page without saying so.

The hook now returns the whole page and the header reports `count`. Page controls
and a page-size selector sit under both views. Page keys extend the existing
`list` key, so every mutation's invalidateQueries still reaches all cached pages
unchanged.

The board paginates with the table rather than fetching every page. That is the
trade-off worth knowing: a Kanban column counts only the current page, so an
empty column does not mean no risks carry that response. A banner says as much,
and the page-size selector goes to 200.

Selection is page-scoped, which the bulk bar now states outright. Deleting a
page's last row steps back a page first, because DRF answers an out-of-range page
with a 404 rather than an empty one.

components/ui/pagination.tsx is upstream shadcn v4 with its two import paths
rewritten. The CLI was not used: it resolves upstream's `cn` import as an npm
package and installs an unrelated one.

Closes #484

chore(core): seed the Risk Register with enough risks to paginate

No seeded threat model carried any risks, so the register was empty in every
development database and its pagination could not be exercised at all.

_seed_risks keys on whether the target model already has risks, not on whether
this run created it. _create_sample_threat_models skips a model that exists, so
a step hung off model creation would never run on a database that had been
seeded before.

Scores are derived through calculate_inherent_score rather than written into the
data, so demo risks cannot drift from what the scoring engine produces.
